claims.claim:
say something accurate early, never contradict it later, and never create legal
exposure or tip off the attacker.

Pre-approved **holding statements** for: service outage of unknown cause, confirmed cyber
  incident under investigation, ransomware, data exposure.
Approval chain: comms lead drafts, technical lead fact-checks, legal approves, exec signs.
Spokesperson named and media-trained; everyone else refers enquiries to the press office.
Every public fact must be **confirmed by forensics**.

"No customer data was accessed" in
  week one is the classic mistake
say "we have not found evidence that..." only if true

Consistency across channels: website, customer emails, support scripts, investor
  disclosure (SEC 8-K) and regulator notifications must not contradict each other.

Do not name the threat actor or confirm ransom details; it complicates negotiation and law
  enforcement work.

Do not publish IOCs or technical detail that reveals what you know while the attacker may
  still be present.
Watch social media and leak sites; the attacker may publish first.

Have a response ready
  for "the group claims to have X TB of data".
Employees: brief them on what to say to customers and remind them not to post.

Archive every published statement with timestamp; regulators and litigants will compare them
with your later findings.
Tabletop inject: a journalist calls the help desk at hour 3.

Was the call routed correctly and
did anyone deviate from the holding line?

coverage: I chose every concrete claim in the skill - all 16 preparation, approval-chain, spokesperson, forensics-confirmation, channel-consistency (including the SEC 8-K disclosure), threat-actor, IOC, leak-site, employee-briefing, statement-archiving and tabletop-inject behaviours with their numbers (week one, hour 3, X TB) - then fetched both listed sources and searched each page for every claim.
suggested_edits: Nothing is contradicted, but neither listed source covers any claim: the csrc.nist.gov page is the SP 800-61r3 publication abstract (CSF 2.0 profile framing, no public-communications guidance) and the NCSC page is the incident-management collection index whose only media reference is 'minimising public and media fall out'. A fix PR should bump version and cite sources that actually state these behaviours - e.g. the full NIST SP 800-61r3 PDF sections on communications and coordination, the NCSC incident-management sub-pages on plans and crisis management (or NCSC ransomware/crisis-communications guidance), and an SEC page on Form 8-K Item 1.05 disclosure for the investor-notification claim - or narrow the claims to what those pages state.
